Parameter estimation
Parameter estimation is the process of guessing a model's parameter values based on measured data.
Theory of parameter estimation and its use in fitting probability distributions to data is a major theme of mathematical statistics. It is applied when there is a random sample from some distribution \(F_\theta\) specified up to a vector of unknown parameters \(\theta\) which need to be determined.
Parameter estimation is used in various fields such as machine learning, signal processing etc.
For instance, imagine we have a coin and we do not know whether it is fair or not. Clearly, the indicator random variable \(X_1\) of getting Heads in one toss of this coin has Bernoulli distribution \(\mathscr{B}(1,p)\). But with what parameter \(p\)? To solve this problem, we can flip the coin a large number of times and somehow use the obtained information to estimate the value of parameter \(p\).
Many families of probability distributions depend on a small number of parameters: for example,
Normal family depends on two parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\);
the Binomial family on a single parameter \(p\).
In general, we consider a family of probability distributions \(F_\theta\) with parameter \(\theta\) from some parameter set \(\Theta \subset \mathbb{R}^k\). When we have some sample from one distribution \(F_\theta\) from that family, we can use the observed data to make inferences about the unknown parameters \(\theta\), i.e., to estimate these parameters.
If \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), we write its probability density function (p.d.f.) as \[ f(x \mid \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp \Bigl(- (x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2\Bigr) \]
Then for a random vector \(\mathbf{X}=(X_1, \dots, X_n)\), where \(X_1\), \(\dots\) ,\(X_n\) are independent identivally distributed random variables with distribution \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), we have \[ f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x} \mid \mu, \sigma^2) = \prod_{k=1}^n f(x_k \mid \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac1{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{n/2}}\exp\Bigl(-\sum(x_k-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2\Bigr) \] In general, we write \(f(x \mid \theta)\) or \(f_\theta(x)\) to indicate that the p.d.f. (or p.m.f.) depends on a parameter \(\theta\). Note that \(\theta\) may be a vector of parameters, e.g., \( \theta = (\mu, \sigma^2)\).
The standard setting
The set of distributions with densities/mass functions \(f_\theta(x)\), \(\theta \in \Theta\), is called the parametric family. Here \(\Theta\) denotes the set of all possible values of parameters \(\theta\);
to model the data, we consider a sample from this parametric family, i.e., the sequence \((X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)\) of i.i.d.  r.v.'s with p.d.f. \(f_\theta\) for an unknown \(\theta\in\Theta\);
data \((x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n)\) give a sample realization, i.e., \(x_k\) is the observed value of \(X_k\).
Example (Tossing a coin). Assume we toss a coin \(n\) times. Then the outcome of this experiment is \(\omega = \omega_1\omega_2\dots \omega_n\), with \(\omega_k = H\) or \(T\) according as the \(k\)th toss returned `Head' or `Tail'. Introduce the random variable \(X_k\) by \[ X_k(\omega) = \begin{cases} 1 & \quad \text{if} \quad \omega_k = H \\0 & \quad \text{if} \quad \omega_k = T \end{cases} \] Then \((X_1,\dots, X_n)\) is a sample from the binomial distribution \(\mathscr{B}(1,p)\); there are \(2^n\) possible realizations \(\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\).
To estimate the parameter of the distribution, we combine observed data into some functions.
Definition (Statistics)
A statistics, \(T(\mathbf{X})\), is a function of the sample \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1,\dots,X_n)\)
Here are examples of statistics: \[ \frac1n(X_1+\dots + X_n), \quad \max_{k}X_k, \quad X_1e^{X_2}+X_3 \]
Definition (Estimator)
An estimator of the parameter \(\theta\) is a statistics \(\widehat{\Theta} = T (\mathbf{X})\), which we use to guess \(\theta\) from observation of \(\mathbf{X}\).
Once the actual data \(\mathbf{x}\) is observed, \(\widehat{\theta} = T (\mathbf{x})\) is the estimate of \(\theta\) obtained via the estimator \(T\).
Note that the estimator is a random variable, while the estimate is the observed value of the estimator.
Example. For instance, if we have data sampled from the normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), a good estimator for the mean \(\mu\) is the sample mean \(\bar{\mathbf{X}}=(X_1+X_2+...+X_n)/n\). Thus for realization of size \(3\) \(X_1=2\), \(X_2=3\), \(X_3=4\) the corresponding estimate of the mean \(\mu\) is \(\hat\mu=3\).
Usually we use capital letters with hat to denote the estimator and small letters with hat to denote the corresponding estimate.
Unbiasedness of estimators
In general, it is intuitively desirable for the expected value of an estimator to be equal (or at least close) to the true parameter value \(\theta\), but this will not always be the case. The bias of an estimator \(\hat\theta\) is defined as the deviation of the expectation from the true value:
\[ \text{Bias} = \mathbb{E}(\hat\Theta)-\theta \]
With everything else being held equal (ceteris paribus), the smallest bias is more preferable. An estimator for which the bias is zero (meaning \(\mathbb{E}(\hat\Theta)=\theta\)) is called unbiased.
Definition (Unbiased estimator)
An estimator \(\widehat\Theta\) of \(\theta\) is said to be unbiased if \(\mathsf{E}(\widehat\Theta) = \theta\).
Example. (Estimating \(p\) for Bernoulli distribution). Suppose \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) are i.i.d. random variables with distribution \(\mathscr{B}(1,p)\) and \(p\) is unknown. Consider the estimator for \(p\) given by \[ \widehat{P}(\mathbf{X}) = \overline{\mathbf{X}} = \frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n X_k \] The estimator \(\widehat P\) is unbiased, since \[ \mathsf{E} \widehat P(\mathbf{X}) = \mathsf{E} \Bigl[\frac1n \sum_{k=1}^n X_k \Bigr] = \frac1n \sum_{k=1}^n \mathsf{E} X_k = \frac1n np = p \] Note that the unbiased estimator is not unique. For example, another unbiased estimator for \(p\) is \[ \widetilde P(\mathbf{X}) = (X_1 + 2X_2)/3. \]

Moment method estimator (text)
Let us now consider some ways to produce estimators. In this section, we consider the moment method estimator.
Observe that if the unknown parameter of \(f(x\mid \theta)\) is its expected value (\(\mathsf{E} X = \theta\)), then an unbiased estimator for \(\theta\) is the sample mean: \[ \widehat\Theta = \overline{\mathbf{X}} = \frac1n(X_1+ \dots + X_n) \]
Example (Bernoulli distribution). If \(X\sim \mathscr{B}(1,p)\), then \[ \mathsf{E} X = 1 \cdot p + 0 \cdot(1-p) = p, \] so that \(\widehat{P}=\overline{\mathbf{X}}\) is the unbiased estimator of \(p\).
Example (Poisson distribution). If \(X \sim \mathscr{P}(\lambda)\), then \(\mathsf{E} X = m_1 = \lambda\).    Therefore, \(\widehat\Lambda:= \widehat m_1 = \overline{\mathbf{X}}\) is the unbiased estimator of \(\lambda\)
These are examples of the moment method estimators.
Definition (Moment metod estimator
Denote by \(m_k:= \mathsf{E} X^k\) the \(k^{\mathrm{th}}\) moment of \(X\) and assume that \(\theta = g(m_1,m_2,\dots,m_r)\) for some function \(g\); then the moment method estimator of \(\theta\) is \[ \widehat\Theta = g(\widehat m_1 ,\widehat m_2, \dots, \widehat m_r), \] with \(\widehat m_k:= (X_1^k + \dots + X_n^k)/n\) denoting the \(k^\mathrm{th}\) sample moment.
Observe that by law of large numbers the \(k^{th}\) sample moment converges to the \(k^{th}\) theoretical moment of the corresponding distribution. Therefore for continuous function \(g\), \(g(\widehat m_1 ,\widehat m_2, \dots, \widehat m_r)\) converges (e.g. in probability) to \(g(m_1,m_2,\dots,m_r)\). This implies that the moment method estimator converges to the true value of  the parameter and so is good in this sense.
Example (MME for geometric distribution). For \(X\) with geometric distribution \(\mathcal{G}(p)\), \(\mathsf{E} X = 1/p\). Therefore \(p = 1/m_1\), whence \[ \widehat P = \frac1{\widehat m_1} = \frac{n}{X_1+ \dots + X_n} \]
Example. (Moment method estimator for the variance). As \(\mathsf{Var} X = \mathsf{E} X^2 - (\mathsf{E} X)^2 = m_2 - m_1^2\), the moment method estimator of the variance \(\sigma^2\) is \[ \widehat \sigma^2 = \widehat m_2 - (\widehat m_1)^2 = \frac1n \sum (X_k - \overline{\mathbf{X}})^2 =: \frac1n S_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}} \] Observe that \begin{align*} \mathsf{E} \Bigl(\sum (X_k - \overline{\mathbf{X}})^2\Bigr) &= \sum \mathsf{E} (X_k - \mu + \mu - \overline{\mathbf{X}})^2 \\ & = n \sigma^2 + n \mathsf{E}(\mu - \overline{\mathbf{X}})^2 + 2\sum \mathsf{E}(\mu - \overline{\mathbf{X}})(X_k - \mu) \\ & = n \sigma^2 - n \mathsf{E}(\mu - \overline{\mathbf{X}})^2 = n \sigma^2 - n \mathsf{Var}(\overline{\mathbf{X}}) \\ & = (n-1) \sigma^2 \end{align*} Therefore often \(S_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}}/(n-1)\) is taken as an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\). And we see that the moment method estimator of variance is not unbiased as \[\mathsf{E}\widehat \sigma^2=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2.\] However, it tends to theoretical variance as \(n\) tends to infinity.
The main advantage of the moment method estimator is that, usually, it is simple to apply. But very often we have several ways to define the function \(g\) which provide different estimators. Therefore, the moment method estimator is often not unique, and then the problem arises, which one to choose.
Example. Consider a sample \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) from normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\). Then there are two natural estimators for the variance. Namely,
as \(\sigma^2 = \mathsf{E}(X_1^2)\), one can take \(\widehat m_2\) as the estimator
as \(\sigma^2 = \mathsf{Var}(X_1)\), one can take \(\widehat m_2 - \widehat m_1^2 = S_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}}/n\) as the estimator.

Desired properties of estimators (text)
As we already discussed, often there are several estimators for the same parameter. Then how to choose the best one? In this section, we consider some characteristics of parameter estimators which allow us to do this (if it is possible).
Recall
Definition
An estimator \(\widehat\Theta\) of \(\theta\) is said to be unbiased if \(\mathsf{E}(\widehat\Theta) = \theta\).
Unbiased estimators \(\widehat\Theta\) are desired, however, also asymptotically unbiased estimators are good
Definition
The estimator \(\widehat\Theta\) of \(\theta\) is asymptotically unbiased if \(\mathsf{E}\widehat\Theta \to \theta\) as \(n\to\infty\).
Example. The MLE estimator \(\widehat\Lambda= 1/\overline{\mathbf{X}}\) of \(\lambda\) in the exponential distribution \(\mathcal{E}(\lambda)\) is biased. Indeed, as we know \(X_1 + \dots + X_n\) has distribution \(\Gamma(n,\lambda)\) and so \(\overline{\mathbf{X}}\ \sim \Gamma(n,n\lambda)\). Therefore, \[ \mathsf{E}\widehat\Lambda = \int_0^{\infty} \frac{(n\lambda)^n t^{n-2}e^{-n\lambda t}\,dt}{\Gamma(n)} = \frac{n\lambda}{n-1}. \] Thus \(\widehat\Lambda\) is not unbiased but it is asymptotically unbiased!
However, unbiasness or asymptotic unbiasness is not all that we need. Let us recall an example.
Example (Estimating \(p\) for Bernoulli distribution).  Suppose \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) are i.i.d. random variables with the distribution \(\mathscr{B}(1,p)\) and \(p\) is unknown. Consider the estimator for \(p\) given by \[ \widetilde P(\mathbf{X}) = (X_1 + 2X_2)/3. \] It is unbiased. But it produces only values \(0,1/3,2/3\) and \(1\). And if for instance, we have a fair coin with probability \(1/2\) of getting 'Heads' then the true value of \(p\) is \(1/2\); thus by using this estimator, it is not possible to get closer to the true value \(1/2\) of the parameter.
Thus not only bias is important. We are interested in such estimators which produce values close to the true value of the parameter.
Definition
An estimator is called consistent if \(\widehat{\Theta} \stackrel{\mathsf{P}}{\rightarrow} \theta\) as \(n \to \infty\).
Clearly, if \(\theta = \mathsf{E}(X_k)\), then \(\widehat\Theta = \overline{\mathbf{X}}\) is consistent but \(\widehat\Theta = \tfrac13X_1+ \tfrac13X_2\) is not.
Usually, consistency is guaranteed by the Law of Large Numbers in combination with the following fact:
If \(\xi_n \stackrel{\mathsf{P}}{\rightarrow} a\) and a function \(g\) is continuous around the point \(a\), then \(g(\xi_n) \stackrel{\mathsf{P}}{\rightarrow} g(a)\) as \(n\to\infty\)
Example. The estimator \(\widehat\Lambda = 1/\overline{\mathbf{X}}\) for \(\lambda\) in \(\mathcal{E}(\lambda)\) is consistent. Indeed, by the law of large numbers \[ \overline{\mathbf{X}} \stackrel{\mathsf{P}}{\rightarrow} \frac1\lambda\] Then using the above fact with the function \(g(t)=1/t\) we get \[ \frac1{\overline{\mathbf{X}}} \stackrel{\mathsf{P}}{\rightarrow} \lambda \] yielding that \(\widehat\Lambda\) is a consistent estimator.
Theorem (Sufficient condition for consistency).
If \(\widehat\Theta\) is asymptotically unbiased and \(\mathsf{Var}(\widehat\Theta)\to0\), then \(\widehat\Theta\) is consistent.
Proof. Since \(\widehat\Theta\) is asymptotically unbiased and \(\mathsf{Var}(\widehat\Theta)\to0\), we have that \[ \mathsf{E}(\widehat\Theta-\theta)^2 = \mathsf{Var}(\widehat\Theta) + (\mathsf{E}\widehat\Theta - \theta)^2 \to 0. \] Thus by the Markov inequality \[ \mathsf{P}(|\widehat\Theta- \theta| \ge \varepsilon) = \mathsf{P}\{(\widehat\Theta - \theta)^2\ge{\varepsilon^2}\} \to 0 \] which by definition means that \(\widehat\Theta\) is a consistent estimator.
Definition (Mean square error)
The expectation \[ \mathsf{E} (\widehat\Theta-\theta)^2 =(\mathsf{E}\widehat\Theta-\theta)^2 + \mathsf{Var} \widehat\Theta \] is called mean square error (MSE)
Clearly, if the MSE of some estimator goes to zero, then this estimator is consistent.
Observe that here \((\mathsf{E}\widehat\Theta-\theta)^2\) is the squared bias of the estimator \(\widehat\Theta\); thus estimators with vanishing MSE should be considered good as they are both asymptotically unbiased and consistent. Thus a natural problem arises to find an estimator of the smallest possible MSE. Very often, this task can uniquely be solved within the class of unbiased estimators (thanks to the Rao-Blackwell theory). However, the general problem is quite difficult since the optimal estimator need not be unbiased, as the following example demonstrate.
Example. Estimators with the lowest mean square error need not be unbiased: for the normal distribution family \(\mathscr{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\),
the MLE for \(\sigma^2\) is \(S_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}}/n\),
the unbiased estimator is \(S_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}}/(n-1)\),
among all estimators of the form \(\alpha S_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}}\), \(S_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}}/(n+1)\) has the smallest mean square error.
